title: Real-time visualization of shear-induced structures in turbulent flow of wormlike micellar solutions and physically interpretable machine-learning prediction of drag reduction
authors: T. A. Nguyen, Van Kuu Nguyen, Van Lap Nguyen
abstract: The role of shear-induced structures (SIS) in surfactant drag reduction (DR) is difficult to verify directly in fully developed turbulent pipe flow. This study combines rheology, pressure-drop measurements, laser-sheet imaging, ultrasonic velocity profiling (UVP), and machine learning in excess-counterion surfactant solutions. Friction was measured in three pipe diameters at Reynolds numbers up to 165 000, high-speed imaging followed SIS formation, and UVP provided mean velocity and turbulence intensity profiles in the 40-mm pipe. A shear-thickening window of 50–3000 s−1 was identified, and the drag-reduction onset in all three diameters fell within it, consistent with near-wall shear triggering SIS nucleation. Sparse structures can appear slightly before measurable DR, whereas abundant SIS occur only within the drag-reducing regime and their growth parallels DR. Velocity profiles in this regime lie above the Newtonian turbulent profile, with enhanced near-wall streamwise fluctuation intensity, in line with the bilayer picture. Three machine-learning models were trained on Reynolds number, pipe diameter, and surfactant concentration, operational inputs independent of the pressure measurement that defines DR. Support vector regression generalized best, and Shapley Additive Explanations analysis ranked features consistently with the shear-controlled interpretation. Overall, the rheology, friction, imaging, and velocimetry results agree with a shear-controlled picture in which SIS formation accompanies drag reduction, and the machine-learning model provides a practical, physically consistent predictor within the tested operating domain. This combined evidence establishes a strong correlation; a causal demonstration would require simultaneous microstructural and turbulence diagnostics, which lie beyond the scope of this study.

title: Implicit Finite-Difference Scheme for Two-Dimensional Flood Modelling Using Shallow-Water Equations
authors: A. Zaporozhets, Vladyslav V. Khaidurov
abstract: Accurate and computationally efficient numerical modelling of shallow-water flows is essential for flood prediction and hydrodynamic risk assessment. This study develops an implicit finite-difference scheme for the numerical solution of the two-dimensional shallow-water equations. First, the main numerical approaches used for shallow-water modelling, including finite-difference, finite-volume, finite-element, and discontinuous Galerkin methods, are analysed in terms of accuracy, stability, treatment of discontinuities, and computational requirements. Based on this analysis, an implicit finite-difference formulation is developed that uses central approximations for spatial derivatives and averages flow variables at cell boundaries. The nonlinear terms are treated using Newton linearization, resulting in an iterative scheme that allows larger time steps than explicit formulations constrained by the Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy condition. The proposed method is implemented in MATLAB as a computational module for two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations. Its performance is demonstrated on a test problem that describes the propagation of an initially localised disturbance in a rectangular computational domain with rigid boundaries. The numerical results demonstrate stable wave propagation, conservation of the modelled flow dynamics, and physically consistent boundary reflections. The developed approach provides a computational basis for further integration of shallow-water hydrodynamic models with spatial data and geographic information systems for flood forecasting and risk assessment. The implicit scheme allowed the release of time steps Δt = 0.1, 0.5 and 0.9, which significantly exceeds the limit stability of the explicit scheme, which, due to the Courant–Friedrichs–Lévy conditions, was limited to the value Δt ≤ 0.01. The simulation results show that the developed scheme provides stable wave growth and physically correct separation from impermeable boundaries for all investigated time step indicators. The obtained water depth profiles at times t = 10, 15, 20 and 25 s illustrate the correct evolution of the initial combustion: the wave front expands symmetrically while preserving the conservative properties of the model hydrodynamics. The numerical solution demonstrates the accuracy and robustness of the proposed implicit finite-difference scheme, even when using time steps that are almost two orders of magnitude larger than those allowed by explicit methods. The results confirm that the developed approach is a robust and computationally efficient tool for hydrodynamic modelling, intended for further integration with geographic information systems in behaviour prediction and risk assessment tasks.

title: A Comparative CFD Analysis of Aerothermal Behaviour of an Orion-Like Capsule in Different Planetary Atmospheres
authors: Sai Veeresh Bandi
abstract: This paper investigates the atmospheric reentry of an Orion-like space capsule across multiple planetary environments under varying wall temperature conditions. To represent these environments, viscous flow modelling is performed using two different approaches to solve the Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) equations. The study focuses on high-altitude aerothermodynamic behaviour over a blunt body in high Mach number flow. The results show that heating characteristics are strongly dependent on the planetary atmosphere and corresponding free-stream conditions. While similar flow assumptions can be applied for Earth and Mars, a significant change in flow behaviour is observed in the case of Titan, despite its comparable atmospheric composition to Earth. This difference is primarily driven by variations in atmospheric density and resulting flow regimes. The findings highlight the importance of accurately selecting free-stream properties and appropriate flow models for predicting aerothermal loads. This work contributes to improving the design and analysis of thermal protection systems for future planetary entry missions.

title: Adaptive N-Subspace Physics-Informed Neural Networks:\\Autonomous Parameter-Space AMR via Vectorized Gradient Conflict Profiling
authors: Kartikey Singh
abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as a foundational paradigm for solving forward and inverse partial differential equations (PDEs). However, standard monolithic architectures suffer from severe optimization pathologies, including global gradient conflict, spectral bias, and artificial numerical dissipation when applied to stiff, multiscale, or discontinuous physical systems. While existing domain decomposition frameworks (e.g., XPINNs, FBPINNs) mitigate localized stiffness, uniform rectilinear partitioning scales exponentially with input dimensionality ($\mathcal{O}(K_0^{d_{\text{in}}})$), inducing a severe curse of dimensionality. Here, we present the \textbf{Adaptive $N$-Subspace Physics-Informed Neural Network (AS-PINN)}, introducing autonomous Parameter-Space Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR). AS-PINN continuously profiles intra-subspace gradient alignment through fast vectorized per-sample pairwise regularized cosine alignment matrices $\mathcal{C}_{k, ij} = \frac{\langle \mathbf{g}_i, \mathbf{g}_j \rangle}{(\|\mathbf{g}_i\|_2 + \epsilon)(\|\mathbf{g}_j\|_2 + \epsilon)}$ using batched reverse-mode automatic differentiation (\texttt{torch.func.vmap}), setting $\mathcal{C}_{k, ij} = 0$ when either gradient has negligible magnitude ($\|\mathbf{g}\|_2 < \epsilon$). When persistent destructive interference is detected via exponential moving averages (destructive clash ratio $\hat{\rho}_k \ge \tau_{\text{clash}}$ and mean off-diagonal alignment $\overline{\mathcal{C}}_k < \tau_{\text{align}}$), the network autonomously cleaves the conflicting parameter manifold, spawning a localized child subspace at the weighted centroid of maximum conflict. To eliminate coordinate aspect-ratio bias in space-time and multi-scale domains, AS-PINN introduces a Dimension-Normalized Anisotropic Bandwidth Matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ and coordinate-normalized separation filtering. To achieve structured second-order optimization, we propose a Two-Stage Discover-and-Deploy AMR Workflow coupled with a Unified Combined Global L-BFGS polish. We provide theoretical proofs establishing Localized Cleavage Invariance, exponential Gauss-Newton Hessian block coupling decay for PDE residual Jacobians, and conditional subspace covering complexity bounds. Across a comprehensive suite of 9 canonical forward, fluid dynamics, quantum mechanics, and high-dimensional benchmark PDEs on NVIDIA CUDA GPUs---including 1D Viscous Burgers Shock, 2D High-P\'eclet Convection ($\boldsymbol{\beta}=(10, 10)$), 2D Quantum Non-Linear Schr\"odinger Soliton, 2D High-Frequency Helmholtz ($k=4\pi$), five-input-dimensional isotropic diffusion (four spatial coordinates plus time), 2D Non-Linear Bratu Thermal Ignition, 2D Kovasznay Flow ($\mathrm{Re}=40$), 2D Lid-Driven Cavity Navier-Stokes ($\mathrm{Re}=100$, achieving $9.39\%$ relative error on streamfunction $\psi$), and 2D Relativistic Klein-Gordon Wave---AS-PINN achieves high accuracy, yielding up to a $\mathbf{725.6\times}$ loss reduction over Standard PINNs, $\mathbf{1.24 \times 10^4\times}$ over PCGrad ($1480\times$ on high-frequency Helmholtz), and $\mathbf{1.79 \times 10^6\times}$ over CAGrad under the reported experimental protocols.

title: Physics-constrained deep learning for prediction of three-dimensional homogeneous isotropic turbulence
authors: Nikita Tsoy, Changhoon Lee
abstract: Three-dimensional turbulence is inherently chaotic and multiscale, posing significant computational challenges for traditional simulation methods, such as direct numerical simulation (DNS), large eddy simulation, and Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes models. Although deep learning (DL) offers a promising data-driven alternative, most existing studies have focused on two-dimensional flows, limiting the physical fidelity and applicability to realistic turbulent processes. This article presents a physically constrained DL framework for predicting three-dimensional homogeneous isotropic turbulence. A neural network was augmented with a Fourier projection to enforce incompressibility and was trained using a two-term loss function that accounted for both the velocity and vorticity fields. The model was trained on DNS data at Reλ = 58, and its generalizability was evaluated on higher-Reynolds-number datasets at Reλ = 92, 160, and 433, where the larger domain was divided into subvolumes matching the training size, the flow fields of which were predicted separately, and then concatenated to reconstruct the full domain. Temporal sampling over several finite lead times enabled the forecasting capability of the model to be evaluated. The proposed approach accurately reproduces key turbulence statistics, resolves three-dimensional vortex structures, and maintains divergence-free velocity fields across prediction horizons up to a lead time of 0.3 Eulerian integral timescale. The results demonstrate that combining data-driven DL with physics-based constraints enables the efficient and reliable prediction of three-dimensional turbulence, balancing computational efficiency and physical fidelity.
